title: Promises, Async/Await and Error Types
subtitle: Promises, Async/Await and Error Types: build, inspect, test, and apply the concept
description: An interactive, dashboard-focused lesson on promises, async/await and error types, with worked code, deliberate debugging, practical transfer, and five explained application questions.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Promises, Async/Await and Error Types: foundations and mental model

Promises, Async/Await and Error Types is not just a syntax topic: it is a way to make the application’s intent explicit. Asynchronous work may complete later or fail. Await the intended operation, handle rejection or errors, and keep loading, success, and failure states distinct. In the Code Academy dashboard, that idea matters because A dashboard module can use explicit types while remembering that external JSON still requires runtime validation. Start by identifying the input, the rule being applied, and the result that a learner should observe. Separate what the code declares from what it actually does at runtime. A name, selector, function, condition, or query should express one clear responsibility. When reading an example, predict its behavior before running or reviewing the output. If the prediction is wrong, trace each meaningful line instead of rewriting everything at once. This habit builds the kind of reasoning that transfers to unfamiliar code, not merely a memory of one sample. The first example introduces the smallest useful version of the idea; later examples test it against variations and edge cases.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Promises, Async/Await and Error Types: An async function returns a Promise even when it returns a plain value
blocks.code:
async function loadTitle(): Promise<string> { return "HTML Foundations"; }
loadTitle().then(console.log);
blocks.output: An async function returns a Promise even when it returns a plain value.

blocks.text: Example 1 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “async function loadTitle(): Promise<string> { return "HTML Foundations"; }”: Declares a reusable operation or program entry point, including the name and expected inputs/result. Line 2 — “loadTitle().then(console.log);”: Continues the example’s expression or control block. Read it in order with the preceding declaration and following result. Expected behavior: An async function returns a Promise even when it returns a plain value. What if a line changes? If the return path is removed, the caller may receive no usable result even though the calculation ran. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A request returns a Promise and the next line reads its result immediately without await or a handler. What is the likely problem?
options: The browser converts every Promise to JSON automatically
The request becomes a CSS animation
The Promise blocks the thread until it succeeds
The code may use the pending asynchronous result instead of the completed value
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: The code may use the pending asynchronous result instead of the completed value. An asynchronous result is not available until its completion path runs.
blocks.reasoning: An asynchronous result is not available until its completion path runs. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Promises, Async/Await and Error Types: await pauses this async function; explicit status and rejection handling separate failure from success
blocks.output: await pauses this async function; explicit status and rejection handling separate failure from success.

blocks.text: Example 2 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “async function loadLesson(): Promise<void> {”: Declares a reusable operation or program entry point, including the name and expected inputs/result. Line 2 — “try { const response = await fetch("/lessons/html_lesson_1.json"); if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Load failed"); console.log(await response.json()); } catch (error) { console.error("Could not load lesson", error); }”: Displays the computed value so the behavior can be observed and checked. Line 3 — “}”: This delimiter opens or closes a block/element so the following statements belong to the intended scope. Expected behavior: await pauses this async function; explicit status and rejection handling separate failure from success. What if a line changes? If task completion, failure handling, or cancellation is ignored, the interface may show stale data or the work may never finish cleanly. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A lesson fetch can fail offline. Which UI states should be distinct?
options: Only a loading spinner that never changes
A single state that always claims the lesson loaded
Loading, success, and failure
Success and failure represented by the same empty string
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Loading, success, and failure. Clear async states avoid presenting failure as success or leaving stale loading indicators.
blocks.reasoning: Clear async states avoid presenting failure as success or leaving stale loading indicators. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Promises, Async/Await and Error Types: implementation, debugging, and edge cases

Implementation quality depends on details that are easy to miss. Asynchronous work may complete later or fail. Await the intended operation, handle rejection or errors, and keep loading, success, and failure states distinct. Compare the expected result with the actual result, then ask which smallest change explains any difference. Check the data type, boundaries, execution order, and assumptions about missing or invalid input. For the Code Academy dashboard, A dashboard module can use explicit types while remembering that external JSON still requires runtime validation. A solution that works only for one perfect input is incomplete. For instance, check empty strings, a zero count, an unavailable resource, an unknown key, or a repeated user action whenever those cases fit the feature. Keep responsibilities small so the cause of a defect can be isolated. The second and third examples show how to make the logic clearer and how to recognize a failure mode. Read the comments and output notes as a guide to reasoning, not as a substitute for inspecting every statement.

blocks.title: Example 3 — Promises, Async/Await and Error Types: Promise
blocks.code:
const results = await Promise.all([Promise.resolve(5), Promise.resolve(2)]);
console.log(results.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));
blocks.output: Promise.all waits for all tasks and fails if one rejects.

blocks.text: Example 3 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “const results = await Promise.all([Promise.resolve(5), Promise.resolve(2)]);”: Waits for or coordinates work that completes asynchronously, so the result is handled at the correct time. Line 2 — “console.log(results.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));”: Displays the computed value so the behavior can be observed and checked. Expected behavior: Promise.all waits for all tasks and fails if one rejects. What if a line changes? If task completion, failure handling, or cancellation is ignored, the interface may show stale data or the work may never finish cleanly. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A slow response for an old search overwrites a newer result. What should be added?
options: A retry loop without a stop condition
A request identity, cancellation, or stale-response guard
A longer fixed delay for every response
A global variable containing only the last character
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: A request identity, cancellation, or stale-response guard. Asynchronous results can arrive out of order; stale work must not replace the latest intent.
blocks.reasoning: Asynchronous results can arrive out of order; stale work must not replace the latest intent. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 4 — Promises, Async/Await and Error Types: A discriminated result makes success and failure data explicit
blocks.code:
type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; message: string };
const result: Result<number> = { ok: false, message: "Offline" };
blocks.output: A discriminated result makes success and failure data explicit.

blocks.text: Example 4 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; message: string };”: Declares a data type or contract that groups fields and/or behavior. Line 2 — “const result: Result<number> = { ok: false, message: "Offline" };”: Declares or assigns a value. The name and type determine how later expressions can use it. Expected behavior: A discriminated result makes success and failure data explicit. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: Several independent requests are all required before rendering. What is a common approach?
options: Await a coordination operation such as Promise.all and handle rejection
Await only the first request and ignore the others
Assume launching requests means they have completed
Convert all errors to empty success values silently
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Await a coordination operation such as Promise.all and handle rejection. A coordination step makes completion requirements explicit and lets the failure path be handled.
blocks.reasoning: A coordination step makes completion requirements explicit and lets the failure path be handled. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Promises, Async/Await and Error Types: applied challenge and mastery check

Professional practice means verifying the requirement from a learner’s point of view. Asynchronous work may complete later or fail. Await the intended operation, handle rejection or errors, and keep loading, success, and failure states distinct. For the Code Academy dashboard, A dashboard module can use explicit types while remembering that external JSON still requires runtime validation. Finish by following a small test sequence: verify a normal case, a boundary case, and a failure case; confirm the page remains understandable; and check that the result matches the requirement rather than merely appearing plausible. Ask what would happen if one important line were removed, changed, or called in the wrong order. Distinguish a syntax error from a logic error and from an interface or data issue. The final sample brings the concept into a compact applied task, and the questions ask for decisions rather than isolated definitions. A strong answer should be supported by a reason and by a test that could prove or disprove the assumption.

Applied challenge: implement a small Code Academy feature that uses promises, async/await and error types. Define the expected behavior in one sentence, identify the input and output, and choose the simplest code pattern above that fits. Test a normal case and an edge case. Then make one controlled change: remove a condition, alter a value, or change an input shape. Record what breaks and explain why. This is the “do and let me do” part of the lesson: the concept becomes memorable when the learner predicts a result, observes it, and explains the difference.

blocks.question: A task may outlive the screen that started it. What should the design consider?
options: Never remove any event listener
Assume the screen remains mounted forever
Make the task mutate whichever page is now visible
Cancellation or stale-result handling and cleanup of listeners/resources
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Cancellation or stale-result handling and cleanup of listeners/resources. Async work should respect the lifetime of the interface or operation that created it.
blocks.reasoning: Async work should respect the lifetime of the interface or operation that created it. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: Lesson recap: Asynchronous work may complete later or fail. Await the intended operation, handle rejection or errors, and keep loading, success, and failure states distinct. Keep the underlying rule in mind when moving to more complex dashboard features. Syntax is the visible surface; reliable reasoning, validation, and testing are the transferable skill.
